title: A 10-year mean delay needs at least 5.96 umol/kg error in a stationary North Pacific to CalCOFI oxygen transfer
abstract: Does a distribution of transport delays fix the failed North Pacific to California oxygen forecast? We fit arbitrary nonnegative annual delay weights to two published oxygen indices within water types on sigma0 26.5. We permit delays of 0–15 years, total weight at most one, and a constant offset of up to 5 umol/kg. The 1999–2015 least-squares fit has a mean delay of 9.02 years and RMS error 0.57 umol/kg, but its 2016–2025 error is 10.98, against 5.33 for persistence. Linear programming proves that any kernel with a 10-year mean needs at least 5.96 umol/kg maximum annual error over 1999–2025. Without that mean constraint the minimum is 3.28, with a feasible mean of 3.77 years. At a training error tolerance of 5 umol/kg, feasible mean delays span 1.47–13.72 years. Thus broadening a close early fit does not fix its forecast, while a short-delay stationary model remains possible. The records do not require a change in transport and do not identify a 10-year mean delay. The stronger limit on long delays depends in part on preliminary 2021–2025 data. These are deterministic bounds for regional indices, not water-parcel ages or statistical confidence limits. Source interpolation, float calibration, spatial sampling and reactive oxygen limit causal inference.
